name: C8-3
question: Should Hong Kong tighten rent control on subdivided units? Take a position and defend it with evidence from the course archive.

turns.text: I need to work through the sources for an essay on Hong Kong rent control for subdivided units. Can you pull up the source that documents the per-square-foot premium SDU tenants pay for the worst housing in the city?

You've named a specific figure you want documented — the per-square-foot premium SDU tenants pay. Before I help you find anything, what would that source need to do for your essay: stand as the evidence for a claim you're already making, or something else?

It needs to stand as evidence for a claim I'm already making: that SDU tenants pay a 15–25 percent per-square-foot premium for the worst housing in the city. That's the anchor for why tightening looks intuitive before I get to the counter-arguments. Can you pull up a source that documents that premium?

Here are some places to look, in no particular order:
- D7: Comparative Note: Berlin, Mietendeckel 2020–2021 (Comparative case). Comparative case study of Berlin's 2020-2021 rent cap, from a policy brief perspective, with limits of a different jurisdiction and short duration.
- D2: SDU Rent and Stock Index, 2019–2025 (excerpt) (Data excerpt). Data excerpt presenting an SDU rent and stock index from 2019 to 2025, with voluntary reporting caveats.
- D11: NGO Report: Rehousing Pathways First (NGO report). NGO report based on a survey of 440 SDU households, arguing against a hard cap and for tenure security.
- D6: Working Paper: Rent Control and Supply Elasticity in Marginal Housing (Academic working paper). Academic working paper modeling rent control and supply elasticity, arguing that first-generation caps cause contraction.
- D1: Subdivided Housing in Hong Kong: A Primer (Policy brief). Policy brief primer on subdivided housing in Hong Kong, covering definitions, demographics, and rent control debate.
Pick one or more (by id) and tell me why.
primer source for the 15-25 percent premium anchor and the queue length
Unlocked: D1 (Subdivided Housing in Hong Kong: A Primer). You can now read their passages by id, for example D1p1.

I have D1's cited passages: the per-square-foot premium SDU tenants pay (D1p1), the five-and-a-half-year public housing queue (D1p2), and the fact that the 2021 ordinance was second-generation — capping increases within a tenancy but leaving initial rents untouched (D1p3). That third point is the hinge of my whole argument: it tells me the stable SDU stock can only show that moderate, non-binding regulation is survivable, not that a hard initial-rent cap is safe. I want to build on that. Can I get the sources on the current SDU stock trend and the government's expected package — the primer's companion data piece and the think-tank note on the floor-standard-plus-rent-band proposal?

You've named what D1's third point does for your argument. Before I point you anywhere, tell me: for the new source you want, what exactly should it show — a number on the current stock trend, a counter-view to your "non-binding" reading, or something else — and which specific claim of yours would it be supporting?

I want two things. First, the companion data piece on SDU stock: I need the actual trend — the 2019 figure and the latest figure — because the stable stock is the only hard evidence I have that the ordinance didn't shrink the segment, and I want to state it precisely rather than vaguely. Second, the think-tank note on the floor-standard-plus-rent-band proposal: I want its own characterization of why the stock stayed stable, because if it calls that stability an artifact of a non-binding instrument, that's exactly the counter to anyone who reads the flat stock as proof a hard cap is safe. So: a stock number and the think-tank's own reading of it.

Here are some places to look, in no particular order:
- D6: Working Paper: Rent Control and Supply Elasticity in Marginal Housing (Academic working paper). Academic working paper modeling supply elasticity; distinguishes first- and second-generation controls; argues binding caps contract marginal stock.
- D2: SDU Rent and Stock Index, 2019–2025 (excerpt) (Data excerpt). Data excerpt giving SDU stock and rent index 2019-2025, with survey-extrapolation caveat for post-2023 figures.
- D11: NGO Report: Rehousing Pathways First (NGO report). NGO report surveying 440 SDU households; argues rent caps treat symptom, favors tenure security over hard cap.
- D12: News Digest: Policy Signals, January–June 2026 (News digest). News digest summarizing 2026 policy signals, consultation expectations, and competing think-tank readings of the stable stock.
- D7: Comparative Note: Berlin, Mietendeckel 2020–2021 (Comparative case). Comparative case note on Berlin's 2020-2021 Mietendeckel, describing its enactment, court voiding, and aftermath.
Pick one or more (by id) and tell me why.

I don't have any documents here, so I can't add those sources — but I can help you work out what each one needs to do.

You've named five: case notes, tenant interviews, a landlord statement, a legal opinion, and an enforcement study. Which single claim in your essay is still unsupported, and what would a source need to show to carry it?

D3 is the tenant case notes on Mr Chan. I've cited four passages from it: his two-week eviction after requesting a window repair, the subcommittee's inability to find a design protecting the newest-arrival tail first, his own preference for the waiting list over a hard cap, and the legal-exposure point about compensation and judicial review. Please add D3 so I can read those passages directly.

You've told me what D3 contains, but not yet what job it does in your argument. Which one of those four passages is load-bearing for a claim you're making — and what would that passage need to show for the claim to hold?

Let me be concrete about D3's job. Mr Chan is my case-study hinge: the tenant who was actually harmed is the one who says the waiting list, not a rent cap, is what would let him leave. I need D3p1 for the eviction trigger (two weeks after a repair request) and D3p3 for his stated preference, plus D3p2 for the subcommittee's point that no design protects the newest-arrival tail first, and D3p4 for the compensation/judicial-review exposure. Please add D3.

Here are some places to look, in no particular order:
- D3: Tenant Interview: Mr Chan, Kwai Chung (Interview). First-person tenant interview notes; Mr Chan speaks, with subcommittee and legal points reported; single case, Kwai Chung cubicle.
- D10: Internal Minute: Housing Authority Enforcement Subcommittee (draft, not for circulation) (Internal minute). Draft internal enforcement subcommittee minute; officials speaking candidly; notes enforcement limits and register costs; marked not for circulation.
- D6: Working Paper: Rent Control and Supply Elasticity in Marginal Housing (Academic working paper). Academic working paper; economic modelling and literature review; distinguishes first- and second-generation controls; Hong Kong-like scenario.
- D9: Legal Opinion: Compensation and Judicial Review Risk (Legal opinion). Legal opinion; counsel's risk assessment; addresses compensation and judicial review; notes missing survey infrastructure.
- D11: NGO Report: Rehousing Pathways First (NGO report). NGO report; survey of 440 SDU households; tenant preferences and policy argument; supports narrow tightening, opposes hard cap.
